newsitem.title: USA: Big July U.S. payrolls jump fuels few wage worries.
newsitem.headline: Big July U.S. payrolls jump fuels few wage worries.

text.p: The U.S. economy continued to add jobs at a startling rate in July but without causing too much concern to U.S. investors since tight labor markets have generated hardly a whiff of inflation, economists said.
The Labor Department reported on Friday that non-farm payrolls grew by 316,000 in July, well above the consensus forecast of 193,000 and June's upwardly revised 228,000.
The unemployment rate retreated from 5.0 percent in June to 4.8 percent, where it last stood in May when it was the lowest level in nearly a quarter century.

Employees clocked in only 34.4 hours, on average, versus 34.7 in June. The workweek often declines in the first month of a quarter, a statistical quirk that economists said is sometimes hard to account for.
"Given the big decline in the workweek, obviously labor inputs are down in spite of a strong number," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank Corp.
Other problematic seasonal factors may have contributed to the big rise in goverment payrolls, which jumped to 19.698 million in July from 19.642 million, according to the Labor Department.
"Seasonal factors boosted teachers on payrolls by 48,000. So, a lot of it is local education payrolls," Berner said.
Construction jobs rose 3,000, retail employment jumped 65,000 and services increased 113,000, including the larger state, local and federal government payrolls.
But factory jobs fell 5,000 last month, and the manufacturing workweek was trimmed to 41.7 hours from 41.8 hours.
"On balance, I think it's a pretty good number," said Wayne Ayers, chief economist at Bank of Boston. "My own hunch is that any negative reaction will be very, very short lived."

"This number is fully consistent with everyone's -- at least (Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenpan's) -- expectations that the economy will pick up a little steam in the third quarter, but not enough to be terribly worrisome," Ayers concluded.
